podcast.title: Session Musician Career Start (1957) and Instrument Switch
podcast.body: Carol K began her career as a studio musician in 1957. She initially played guitar but made a significant switch to bass in 1963, a time when women rarely played the instrument professionally. Despite societal norms, her dedication to securing gigs led her to master the bass, pioneering the role for women. "She started working in studios in 1957, switching from guitar to bass in 1963."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Switch from Guitar to Bass in 1963
podcast.body: Kaye began working in studios in 1957 as a guitarist but switched to bass in 1963. This was a bold move at a time when bass was not considered "a lady's instrument," yet she embraced the opportunity for gigs, defying gender norms. "She started working in studios in 1957, switching from guitar to bass in 1963. And let's say no woman played bass in 1963. She was just not a lady's instrument, but she didn't care if there were gigs to be had as a session bass player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Did Not Play on "Be My Baby"
podcast.body: Despite claims in some sources, Carol Kaye did not play bass on The Ronettes' "Be My Baby." AFM session sheets confirm that the bass players on the track were Ray Pohlman and Jimmy Bond. "So, Carol Kay did not play on this record, and we know that because we have the AFM session sheet, which show that the bass players on the track were Ray Pullman and Jimmy Bond."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Extensive Collaborations with Artists
podcast.body: Carol Kaye's session credits include playing with Nancy Sinatra, The Monkees, Ray Charles, Sonny & Cher, Glen Campbell, Neil Young, Frank Zappa, and Tina Turner, underscoring her broad influence and demand. She also played with Frank Black of the Pixies on his 2006 record "Fast Man Rader". "Nancy Sinatra, the monkeys, Ray Charles, Sonny and Cher, Glenn Campbell, Neil Young, Frank Zap, a Tina Turner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Collaborations with Major Artists
podcast.body: Carol K's prolific career saw her collaborate with an almost endless list of legendary artists across various genres. Her basslines can be heard on tracks by Glenn Campbell, Neil Young, Frank Zappa, Ray Charles, and Tina Turner. "Glenn Campbell, Neil Young, Frank Zappa, Ray Charles, Tina Turner. The list is nearly endless."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Movie and TV Soundtrack Work
podcast.body: Carol Kaye's contributions extended to numerous movie soundtracks, including "The Thomas Crown Affair," "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid," and at least one "Planet of the Apes" movie. She also played on themes for "Jerry Harry," "Wonder Woman," "Mash," "Mission Impossible," and "The Brady Bunch," showcasing her diverse work in film and television. "And I hadn't mentioned all the movie soundtracks, the Thomas Crown Affair, butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, at least one planet of the Apes movie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Famous Studio Bass Player
podcast.body: Carol Kaye is recognized as the bass player for The Wrecking Crew, which is widely regarded as the most famous studio outfit of all time. Her work on the Fender Precision Bass helped define the sound of countless hit records. "Carol K, the bass player for the most famous studio outfit of all time, The Racking Crew."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Integral Member of The Wrecking Crew
podcast.body: Within a few years of switching to bass, Carol K became a key member of The Wrecking Crew, an elite group of in-demand studio musicians in Los Angeles. These top-notch players were known for their ability to perform in any musical style at any time, and were called upon when only the highest caliber of musicianship would suffice. "Within a few years, she was part of a group of studio musicians known as The Rucking Crew, some really top-notch players who were called in when only the best would do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Later Career Work with Frank Black and Matthew Sweet
podcast.body: Demonstrating her enduring career, Carol K played on Frank Black of the Pixies' 2006 record "Fast Man Raider." She also collaborated with Matthew Sweet in 1999, appearing on his album "In Reverse" on the song "Faith in You," further solidifying her legacy as an important figure in rock history. "She even played with Frank Black of the Pixies on a 2006 record called Fast Man Raider."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: One of the Most Heard Bass Players
podcast.body: Carol Kaye is considered one of the most heard bass players in history, with a modest estimate of appearing on 10,000 different recordings. Her prolific session work has made her an ubiquitous presence in recorded music across decades and genres. "A modest guess is that she appears on 10,000 different recordings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Renowned Session Musician
podcast.body: Carol Kaye was one of the most acclaimed bass players and session guitarists of the 1960s, contributing to hundreds of classic records for artists including The Beach Boys, Phil Spector, and Frank Zappa. She was notably the only woman consistently engaged in session work on a rock instrument in Los Angeles during that era. "Ms. Kay was one of the great bass players of the 60s, and also one of the better session guitarists. She played on hundreds of records in the 60s, including many, many classics from The Beach Boys, Spectre, Frank Zapper and others, and she was the only woman getting regular session work in LA on a rock instrument."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Unreliable Credits and False Claims
podcast.body: Carol Kaye is described as an unreliable and dishonest source regarding her session credits. While some memory lapses over five decades are acknowledged (e.g., "Good Vibrations"), she has made numerous unsubstantiated claims, such as playing on almost the entire recorded works of Motown's James Jamerson (claiming secret tape shipments from Detroit to LA, denied by Motown staff) or The Monkees' "I'm a Believer" (recorded in New York by New York musicians). When confronted with falsehoods, she responds with abuse and libel on her website rather than admitting error. "Carol Kay is not only an unreliable source about what records she played on, she has an utterly dishonest one."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
